title: Artificial intelligence for literature reviews: opportunities and challenges
extended_summary:
This paper reviews how artificial intelligence is being used to support systematic literature reviews (SLRs), focusing especially on the screening and data-extraction phases. The authors argue that SLRs are labor-intensive, slow, and expensive, and that AI methods such as machine learning, natural language processing, large language models, and knowledge graphs may help semi-automate parts of the process. The review is not about educational interventions or student learning outcomes; it is about research tools for literature review workflows.

The authors conduct a PRISMA-style systematic review of SLR tools and analyse 21 tools using a framework with 34 features, including 11 AI-specific features. They examine tools for screening, extraction, and more recent LLM-based systems that assist with literature search and academic writing. The paper compares tools by AI approach, text representation, human interaction, input requirements, execution mode, research field, and pre/post-screening support, as well as more general software features such as deduplication, collaboration, protocol support, and export functions.

There is no participant sample in the educational sense; the units of analysis are software tools and prior survey papers. The context is scholarly research practice across domains, with particular attention to biomedical and non-biomedical systematic reviewing. The authors identify trends such as continued reliance on machine-learning classifiers for screening, increasing use of embeddings, limited support for extraction, and emerging incorporation of LLMs into search and writing support.

The main conclusion is that AI-enhanced SLR tools show substantial promise but remain uneven in capability, usability, and evaluation quality. The authors highlight three major challenges for the field: integrating advanced AI methods such as LLMs and knowledge graphs, improving usability, and developing standardized evaluation frameworks. For the user's verification task, this paper is not the alleged 2026 high-school ChatGPT motivation/writing trial, contains no student experiment, no random assignment of learners, and no motivation or writing outcome statistics. It should therefore be excluded from any quantitative synthesis of ChatGPT-based writing feedback in high school because it is off-topic and not a primary intervention study.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a review/survey paper about AI tools for literature reviews, not an empirical study of a K-12 educational intervention. It contains no randomized student experiment, no motivation or writing outcomes, and no extractable causal effect for ChatGPT-based writing feedback in high school.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests possible workflow benefits for researchers using AI-supported literature review tools, but it provides no direct outcome effect estimates and no K-12 learner impact evidence. Any impact is therefore unclear for the target synthesis context.

interventions.use_case: AI-enhanced tools for systematic literature reviews, including machine-learning and LLM-based systems for screening papers, extracting information, literature search, and academic writing support; this is not an educational learner-facing intervention.

finding.finding_summary: This paper is a narrative/systematic review of 21 SLR tools and 11 recent LLM-based research tools, arguing that AI can support screening, extraction, search, and writing in literature reviews. However, it does not report pooled quantitative effect sizes, sample-based comparisons, or experimental estimates of productivity gains; findings are descriptive and tool-feature based rather than empirical impact estimates.
finding.measure: Tool capabilities and AI feature coverage for systematic literature review workflows
finding.study_size: n=21 SLR tools reviewed; plus 11 LLM-based research tools discussed
